description: Children are not just miniature adults. How a child's unique spinal anatomy and biomechanics affect a spinal cord injury claim.
shortAnswer: Children are not just miniature adults. Their anatomy and biomechanics are unique, and this is nowhere more true than in the cervical spine. It is imperative that your attorney have an understanding of both the unique anatomy and biomechanics that affect your child's injury claim.

faq.q: Why is a child's spinal cord more easily injured in a car accident?
faq.a: A child's spinal column has up to 2 inches of "play", while the spinal cord has more like a mere quarter inch. In a motor vehicle accident the spinal column may flex in one or more directions that exceeds the flexibility of the child's spinal cord. This can cause grave injury.

faq.q: What are the most common spinal injuries in children?
faq.a: Some of the most common injuries to the spine in children are: facet dislocations, posterior ligament injuries, and wedge compression fractures. In children under 8 years of age, spinal cord injuries are most often located in the cervical spine (the neck).

faq.q: What does biomechanics mean in a child injury claim?
faq.a: Biomechanics, in the legal arena, refers to the proof of the mechanism of injury (what factors, what forces, what objects caused the injury and how?).

faq.q: Do insurance companies argue that injured children will bounce back?
faq.a: Many insurance companies deny or seek to minimize the impact of an injury on a young child. They argue that the children are more resilient than adults and can be expected to "bounce back" more quickly. Your attorney must have the specialized knowledge to disabuse the insurer of those misconceptions.
